text: The Constitution of Pakistan (Urdu: آئینِ پاکستان, romanised: Ā'īn-e-Pākistān), also known as the 1973 Constitution, is the supreme law of Pakistan, guiding the country’s legal framework, political culture, and institutional structure. Drafted by Zulfikar Ali Bhutto with input from opposition parties, it was unanimously approved by the 5th Parliament on 10 April 1973 and ratified on 14 August 1973. It establishes a federal parliamentary republic with Islam as the state religion and outlines the separation of powers among a bicameral legislature, an executive led by the Prime Minister, and an apex judiciary headed by the Supreme Court. The President serves as a ceremonial Head of State. The first six articles define the political system as a federal parliamentary republic and affirm Islam as the state religion. The Constitution mandates that all laws conform to Islamic injunctions from the Quran and Sunnah, and establishes institutions such as the Shariat Court and the Council of Islamic Ideology for interpreting and applying Islamic principles. It provides fundamental rights including freedom of speech, religion, press, movement, association, thought, life, liberty, property, and the right to bear arms, with due process rooted in British common law. The Constitution establishes a bicameral Parliament with the National Assembly as the lower house and the Senate as the upper house, ensuring equal provincial representation. It sets eligibility requirements for the President and Prime Minister—only Muslims of at least forty-five years of age—and prohibits laws that are repugnant to Islam. The Constitution introduces the Council of Common Interests to manage inter-provincial policy issues, including water distribution, and the National Finance Commission to regulate revenue sharing between the federation and provinces. It also promotes local government, women’s participation, minority protection, and social and economic well-being. The Constitution was adopted on 23 March 1956 as the first constitution, celebrated annually as Republic Day, and was later abrogated in 1958 and 1972. The 1962 Constitution introduced a presidential system and concentrated power in the President, but was suspended in 1969 and abrogated in 1972. The 1973 Constitution, framed by elected representatives, restored a parliamentary democracy with executive power in the Prime Minister. It has been amended 23 times, with three amendments failing to pass Parliament. The current promulgated Constitution is the 7th longest in the world, containing 56,240 words. The Objectives Resolution, passed in March 1949, was incorporated as a preamble into all subsequent constitutions and affirmed democracy and Islamic principles. Jinnah, in a 1948 radio talk, emphasized that the future constitution would be democratic and rooted in Islamic ideals. The 1973 Constitution was formally adopted on 2 February 1973, ratified unanimously on 19 April 1973, and came into full effect on 14 August 1973. On that day, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto was elected Prime Minister after relinquishing the presidency to Fazal-i-Ilahi. The Constitution includes provisions for individual equality, prohibition of slavery, fair trial, and safeguards against discrimination in services and access to public places. It also preserves Urdu as the national language and English as the official language, while protecting all other languages, scripts, and cultures. The Constitution is divided into parts and includes schedules that categorize governmental activities and policies. Amendments to the Constitution require a two-thirds majority in both houses of Parliament, unlike earlier constitutions. The Constitution defines Pakistan as a Federation of Four Provinces and establishes a delicate balance between traditionalist and modernist elements, reflecting compromises on religious rights and humanism.

The Constitution of Pakistan establishes an Islamic way of life, promotes local government, ensures full participation of women in national life, protects minorities, advances social and economic well-being, and strengthens ties with the Muslim world to achieve international peace. Fundamental Rights include security of person, safeguards against arrest and detention, prohibition of slavery and forced labour, freedom of movement, association, speech, religion, and protection of religious institutions, non-discrimination in access to public places and services, and preservation of languages, scripts, and cultures. The judiciary holds full supremacy over other state organs. Urdu is declared the national language and English the official language, with all other languages preserved by the Constitution. Key Islamic principles from the 1956 Articles were incorporated into the Constitution. The Constitution is divided into parts containing individual articles, and schedules list governmental bureaucratic activities and policies. Unlike previous documents, the Constitution cannot be altered directly; instead, amendments are passed through Parliament requiring a two-thirds majority in both houses, and certain federal-related amendments must be ratified by a majority of provincial legislatures. As of 2019, 25 amendments have been made. The Eighth (1985) and Seventeenth (2004) Amendments shifted the government to a semi-presidential system, while the Eighteenth Amendment (2010) reversed this, restoring a parliamentary republic and defining attempts to subvert, abrogate, or suspend the Constitution as high treason. The second amendment (1974) declared Ahmadis to be non-Muslims and was passed unanimously by Parliament. The Twenty-Fifth Amendment incorporated the Federally Administered Tribal Areas into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. In 2017, the Twenty-Seventh Amendment Bill, aimed at implementing recommendations of the Parliamentary Committee on Electoral Reforms, failed to secure required majorities or presidential assent and was not adopted. In 2024, the Twenty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act, enacted on 21 October, introduced landmark judicial reforms focusing on the Supreme Court and High Courts. In 2025, the Twenty-Seventh Amendment Bill proposed changes to Article 243, reflecting decades of shifts in civil-military authority: the 1985 Revival of the Constitutional Order gave the president control over military appointments, the 13th Amendment restored this to the prime minister, the 17th Amendment reversed it, and the 18th Amendment (2010) re-empowered the prime minister. The 27th Amendment proposed abolishing the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Committee and making the Chief of Army Staff, with life-long constitutional immunities, the Chief of Defence Forces, a move critics argue further consolidates military authority. It also proposed giving the prime minister the power to appoint or remove Supreme Court judges and establishing a Federal Constitutional Court, which analysts say would reduce the Supreme Court’s power. After the bill passed in November, two senior Supreme Court judges, Syed Mansoor Ali Shah and Athar Minallah, resigned in protest, citing 'crippled judicial independence.' The Constitution begins with the assertion that sovereignty over the universe belongs to Allah alone, and that the authority of the people of Pakistan is a sacred trust. It establishes a democratic order where the state functions through elected representatives, upholds Islamic principles of democracy, freedom, equality, tolerance, and social justice, enables Muslims to live according to Quranic and Sunnah teachings, ensures minorities can freely practice their religions and develop their cultures, and creates a federal structure with autonomous provinces. Fundamental rights include equality, opportunity, and before the law, social, economic, and political justice, and freedom of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship, and association, subject to law and public morality. The Constitution guarantees safeguards for minorities and backward classes, ensures judicial independence, and protects the integrity of Pakistan’s territories, including sovereign rights over land, sea, and air. The people of Pakistan, cognizant of their responsibilities before Allah and humanity, and inspired by Quaid-i-Azam Mohammad Ali Jinnah’s vision of a democratic state based on Islamic social justice, adopt, enact, and give this Constitution through their representatives in the National Assembly. All Members of the National Assembly (MNAs) from West Pakistan elected in the 1970 general election signed the Constitution except Mian Mahmud Ali Kasuri (PPP, Lahore-III), Abdul Hayee Baloch (NAP(W), Kalat-I), Abdul Khaliq Khan (PPP, Mardan), Haji Ali Ahmed Khan (PPP, Hyderabad-IV), and Nizamuddin Haider (CML, Bahawalpur-I). Sahibzada Muhammad Nazeer Sultan (MJUP, Jhang-III) was the last MNA elected in 1970 and one of the last signatories of the 1973 Constitution. Unlike the 1956 Constitution, which included 23 Hindus, 2 Christians, and 2 women in its creation, the 1973 Constitution had no representation from minorities or women.
